key_insight: Case-specific, clinician-authored rubrics enable clinically valid and economically scalable evaluation of clinical AI; LLM-generated rubrics can approximate clinician agreement when applied across 823 clinical encounters, supporting faster iterative evaluation.
problem_solved: Reduces dependence on slow, expensive per-instance expert review by providing a scalable, clinically grounded rubric methodology that is sensitive to iterative changes in clinical AI systems.
method: Clinicians author concise, case-specific rubrics that define task-relevant scoring criteria and acceptable variations.
LLMs are used to generate or apply rubrics at scale and produce automated scores; outputs are compared against clinician judgments.
Validation across 823 clinical encounters measuring inter-rater agreement, operational cost/time trade-offs, and sensitivity to iterative model changes.
impact: Provides AI/ML teams a practical evaluation pipeline that preserves clinical validity while dramatically reducing expert labor, enabling safer, faster iteration and deployment of clinical AI systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: clinician authors rubric → LLM applies rubric → comparison/validation across encounters (823) to show workflow.
Agreement chart: bar or heatmap comparing clinician vs LLM agreement rates (inter-rater metrics) across encounter subsets.
Cost/time comparison: side-by-side bars showing per-instance expert review vs rubric+LLM workflows for scalability.
Icon set: clinician (authorship), checklist (rubric), robot/LLM (automation), and shield/heart (clinical safety)
paper_title: Case-Specific Rubrics for Clinical AI Evaluation: Methodology, Validation, and LLM-Clinician Agreement Across 823 Encounters
paper_authors: Aaryan Shah, Andrew Hines, Alexia Downs, Denis Bajet, Paulius Mui
